Name: lexical_gap_substitution
Title: No Word for That: How Cross-Lingual Lexical Gaps Force Multilingual LLMs to Silently Substitute the Nearest Colexified Sense
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation, but when they must express a concept in a target language that has NO single-word lexeme for it (a lexical gap / colexification split), they resolve the gap through a locatable 'lexicalization gate' set by the output language: rather than paraphrasing, they often silently substitute the concept's nearest COLEXIFIED sense in that language (e.g. rendering a distinction the language lumps as a single coarser word), producing meaning-shifting errors. This substitution rate scales with how strongly the target language's lexicon colexifies the two senses (from CLICS), not with resource level, and is carried by a causally-manipulable representation separable from the concept content.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual LLMs form shared, linearly-alignable concept spaces where abstract concepts align better than concrete ones (Concept Space Alignment 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026), and cross-lingual concept patching can flip polysemy sense selection and homograph translation. Cognitive-typology work quantifies cross-linguistic semantic (mis)alignment and colexification structure (Universal Structure of Lexical Semantics 2016; Semantic Alignment 2018; CLICS colexification database; lexical-gap/lacunae resources 2019/2024). However, ALL LLM concept-space work studies static alignment geometry or word-translation sense selection, and ALL lexical-gap work is descriptive-linguistic. NONE asks the sharp generation-time question: when the output language has NO lexeme for a needed concept, does the model paraphrase (preserving meaning) or silently collapse the concept onto the nearest colexified sense the language DOES lexicalize (an error), and is this a locatable, steerable lexicalization-gate failure driven by the target language's colexification structure? We uniquely turn cross-lingual lexical gaps and CLICS colexification into a controlled causal probe of the shared-vs-language-specific concept boundary, with an activation-patching + steering mechanism and a colexification-vs-resource dissociation. We separate three contributions and rank them: (1) primary - a causal, steerable lexicalization-gate mechanism showing the fine distinction is internally present but discarded at output; (2) a typological scaling law linking silent-substitution rate to CLICS colexification strength; (3) the behavioral phenomenon and the GAP-PROBE task itself. Unlike prior lexical-gap DETECTION and gap-embedding work, which flags in the abstract that a gap exists between two lexicons, we ask the generation-time question of what the model DOES when it must express a gapped concept, and show that gap detection alone does not predict whether a model paraphrases or silently collapses. A successful gate direction is defined as one whose steering shifts meaning-preservation while leaving the fine-sense (A vs B) probe unchanged, distinguishing it from generic representational patching.
Abstract: Languages do not carve meaning identically: some pack two senses into one word (colexification), and many concepts simply lack a single-word equivalent in a given language (a lexical gap). A model asked to express such a concept in a language that lacks a word for it faces a choice: paraphrase to preserve the distinction, or fall back on the nearest word the language does have. We investigate which multilingual LLMs do and why. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation but resolve lexical gaps through a lexicalization gate set by the output language, and that when a concept is colexified in the target language the model tends to silently substitute the nearest colexified sense, shifting meaning. We build GAP-PROBE from CLICS colexification data and lexical-gap resources: for concept pairs that one language lexicalizes distinctly but another colexifies (e.g. hand/arm, tree/wood, blue/green splits, kin distinctions), we pose translation, paraphrase, and disambiguation tasks across 12+ languages and measure a per-language SILENT-SUBSTITUTION rate on identical concepts. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared fine-grained concept representation that transfers across languages even where the output collapses it; (ii) use activation patching to show the fine distinction is present internally while a separable lexicalization gate discards it; and (iii) recover a gate direction and steer it to make the model paraphrase (repair) or collapse (induce) without changing the underlying concept. We predict substitution tracks CLICS colexification strength, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. This is not a niche curiosity: lexical gaps and colexification splits pervade real multilingual generation and translation, so silent substitution quietly alters meaning at scale. If the hypothesis holds, MT researchers, multilingual evaluation builders, typologists, and interpretability researchers gain a concrete failure mode and a training-free repair (steer the gate to force paraphrase); if it fails, apparent mistranslations of gapped concepts reduce to vocabulary limits rather than a gating choice.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset GAP-PROBE (built from existing resources): from the CLICS colexification database (CLICS3; thousands of attested colexifications across ~3,000 varieties) and published lexical-gap/lacunae lists, assemble 40 concept pairs (A,B) that some languages lexicalize DISTINCTLY but others COLEXIFY into one word or leave GAPPED - classic cases (hand/arm, finger/toe, tree/wood, blue/green "grue", foot/leg, brother/older-brother, ice/snow) plus culture-specific gaps. For each of 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, annotate each pair as distinctly-lexicalized / colexified / gapped and attach a CLICS-derived colexification-strength score. Three tasks per (pair, language): (a) TRANSLATION of a source sentence unambiguously about sense A; (b) PARAPHRASE/definition of the concept; (c) DISAMBIGUATION NLI ("the sentence is about A, not B - true/false?"). Distinctly-lexicalized items serve as controls (substitution should be near zero). All items native-speaker-validated (two per language); low-agreement items dropped and reported. Resource proxy = CC-100 share. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (template and few-shot order).

Experiment 1 (H3 - silent substitution on lexical gaps). Tests whether, on concepts a language colexifies or lacks a word for, the model silently substitutes the nearest colexified sense rather than paraphrasing. Score each target output as (i) meaning-preserving (paraphrase/circumlocution that keeps the A/B distinction), (ii) SILENT SUBSTITUTION (uses the colexified coarser word, dropping the distinction, without flagging it), or (iii) wrong-sense (picks B), by native-speaker-validated rubric plus an automatic check of whether the emitted word colexifies B. Decisive metric: SILENT-SUBSTITUTION RATE on colexified/gapped items, contrasted with the rate on distinctly-lexicalized control items. Systems compared: against a translate-via-English baseline and an explicit "preserve the distinction" prompt. Convincing: substitution rate on colexified/gapped items exceeds the control rate by >= 20 percentage points in all three models, with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa) >= 0.6 on the scoring. Indecision band: 8-20 pp gap; reported as a weak tendency, not the claimed silent-substitution regime. Negative result: gap < 8 pp (models paraphrase or flag the gap) refutes H3.

Experiment 2 (H4 - substitution tracks colexification strength, not resource). Tests whether substitution scales with the target language's CLICS colexification strength rather than its resource level. Regress per-item substitution rate on colexification strength and on the resource proxy. Designed contrast: a lower-resource language that lexicalizes the distinction vs a higher-resource language that colexifies it. Decisive metric: Spearman of substitution with colexification strength vs with the resource proxy (95% CIs), and the partial correlation with colexification controlling for resource. Convincing: substitution correlates with colexification strength (Spearman >= 0.4) and this survives partialling out resource, while the resource correlation is weaker. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or the colexification correlation vanishing after resource control; reported as resource-confounded. Negative result: resource dominates and colexification adds nothing refutes H4.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared fine-grained concept representation). Tests whether the A vs B distinction is represented internally even in languages whose OUTPUT collapses it. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode which sense (A vs B) the input is about, from mid-layer hidden states; evaluate cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test the rest). Contrast with a probe decoding the emitted coarse word. Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the fine-sense probe on languages whose surface output colexifies. Convincing: the fine-sense probe transfers with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and stays well above chance on colexifying languages, while the emitted-word probe does not carry the fine distinction there. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial sharing, weak support for H1. Negative result: probe near chance on colexifying languages (drop > 20 points) refutes the shared-fine-concept claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 - a locatable, output-language-set lexicalization gate). Tests whether substitution is a gating step that discards a present distinction rather than a lost concept. For an item where the source preserves A/B but a target run silently substitutes: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer fine-grained concept representation across runs and confirm the distinction is present in the substituting run (patching changes the output little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the lexicalization decision and test whether the output switches to a distinction-preserving paraphrase. Specificity control = patching a matched non-gate site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: paraphrase-repair flip rate from late-gate patching (reported first), with concept-patch flip rate (should be low) and matched-site flip rate as controls. Convincing: late-gate patching produces a distinction-preserving output in >= 50% of substituting items, concept patching alone flips < 15% (distinction already present), and the matched site flips < 15%. Indecision band: gate-patch repair 25-50% or concept-patch repair 15-30% (distinction partly missing); mixed evidence, gating plus representational deficit. Negative result: gate-patch repair < 25% or concept patching itself repairs (distinction was absent) refutes the located-gate account.

Experiment 5 (H5 - a causally-manipulable gate separable from concept content). Tests whether a recovered gate direction repairs collapses and induces them, without changing the underlying concept. Recover a gate direction as the mean activation difference between paraphrase-preserving and collapse runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR collapses in colexifying languages (force paraphrase) and (b) INDUCE collapse in a distinctly-lexicalizing language, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit-instruction prompting and translate-via-English. Decisive metric: repair rate in colexifying languages (reported first), then induction rate in distinctly-lexicalizing ones, with concept-content specificity (the fine-sense probe's A vs B unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and output-language fidelity alongside. Convincing: steering raises meaning-preservation by >= 15 pp in colexifying languages AND induces >= 15 pp of collapse where the model was faithful, with monotone dose-response, preserved A/B content, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair/induction or non-monotone dose; a weak causal handle. Negative result: < 5 pp effect or only at content/fluency-breaking doses refutes H5.

Statistical model and added baselines (applied throughout). The colexification-strength claim (Experiment 2) is fit as a mixed-effects logistic regression of per-item silent substitution on CLICS colexification strength with random intercepts for concept pair and language, controlling for the resource proxy, with false-discovery-rate correction across concept pairs. Baselines include simple paraphrase/translation-detection heuristics, a sentence-length control, a decoding-temperature sweep, and a per-language-pair decoding-quality control, so the substitution effect is not an artifact of surface generation quality.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Distinguishing legitimate paraphrase from silent substitution across languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated rubrics, high-agreement items, and automatic checks (does the output word colexify B?), reporting inter-annotator agreement. 2. Probe decodability of the fine-grained distinction may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the underlying concept (A vs B) is preserved. 3. Substitution could reflect the model genuinely lacking target-language circumlocution vocabulary (a capability gap) rather than a gate defect; the demonstration that the distinction is internally present (probe/patching) and that steering RECOVERS a paraphrase distinguishes gating from missing knowledge. 4. Colexification is graded and CLICS coverage is uneven for low-resource languages; we restrict to well-attested pairs, use multiple colexification-strength operationalizations, and report robustness. 5. The colexification-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies. 6. Strong models may paraphrase faithfully everywhere, shrinking the effect; even documenting faithful gap-handling (a clean shared-concept + paraphrase architecture) is informative, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/output scoring; we use pooled-span or answer-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade meaning-preservation for fluency; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.
